extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, psychology, and social/scientific method interested in the possibility and methodology of a science of human nature
extracted.subtask_description: Argument and methodological guidance about when and how the study of thoughts, feelings, and actions can be a science: defines laws of mind, gives general laws (association, reproduction of impressions), discusses relation to physiology, and prescribes inductive/experimental methods for establishing mental laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Criteria for a subject to be a science
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted, in themselves, to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws, although those laws may not have been discovered, nor even be discoverable by our existing resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by meteorology and tidology: a subject may be a science even if imperfect or not exact, provided there are regular laws. A science may be practically useful to the extent its principal causes are observable and the effects predictable from them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceptability of approximate generalizations in social inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: An approximate generalization is, in social inquiries, for most practical purposes equivalent to an exact one; that which is only probable when asserted of individuals may be certain when affirmed of masses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because many social phenomena depend mainly on general causes rather than idiosyncratic particulars, approximate laws suffice for political and social science; allowance must be made for probable inaccuracy when applying them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scientific standard for the science of human nature
rubrics_metrics.description: The science of Human Nature exists in proportion as the approximate truths (practical knowledge of mankind) can be exhibited as corollaries from the universal laws of human nature on which they rest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: To be genuinely scientific, approximate empirical generalizations must be connected deductively to underlying causes, showing their limits and allowing deduction of results for new circumstances rather than remaining mere empirical rules.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of the 'laws of mind'
rubrics_metrics.description: By the laws of mind are meant the laws according to which feelings (thoughts, emotions, volitions, sensations) generate one another: i.e., the uniformities of succession among mental states.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This distinguishes laws of mind (mental antecedents producing mental states) from laws of body (states of body producing sensations). The laws concern mental phenomena themselves and their sequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Classification of causes of mental states
rubrics_metrics.description: All states of mind are immediately caused either by other states of mind, or by states of body.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When produced by other mental states the relevant rule is a law of Mind; when produced directly by bodily states (e.g., sensations), the law belongs to physiology (law of Body). This classification guides whether psychological or physiological methods are primary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Necessity of studying mental successions directly
rubrics_metrics.description: Because we are ignorant of the characteristics of the nervous states that supposedly precede mental states, the successions which obtain among mental phenomena must be studied in the mental phenomena themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Even if mental laws are derivative from physiology, they cannot currently be deduced from physiological laws; therefore psychology must use observation and experiment on mental phenomena rather than infer everything from physiology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of experimental/observational methods in psychology
rubrics_metrics.description: The simple or elementary Laws of Mind have been ascertained by the ordinary methods of experimental inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Psychological laws should be established by experiment and observation, and complex laws should be built from elementary observed laws using induction and controlled methods.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law: Reproduction of impressions as ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Whenever any state of consciousness has once been excited in us, an inferior degree of the same state of consciousness (an idea) is capable of being reproduced without the original cause being present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: remembering sights, feelings, or creations of imagination. This is Hume’s formulation that every mental 'impression' has its 'idea' and underpins memory and imagination phenomena.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laws of Association (similarity, contiguity, intensity/frequency)
rubrics_metrics.description: Ideas or secondary mental states are excited by impressions or other ideas according to certain laws: (1) similar ideas tend to excite one another; (2) when two impressions have been frequently experienced together or in immediate succession, one tends to excite the other (contiguity); (3) greater intensity in impressions is equivalent to greater frequency in rendering them mutually excitable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are the elementary laws from which more complex mental sequences and habits are generated; they should be studied experimentally and applied to explain memory, habit, belief formation, and emotional responses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mental chemistry (generation of complex ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: When many impressions or ideas operate together, they sometimes combine in a way analogous to chemical combination, producing complex ideas that may appear simple and are generated rather than merely composed from simpler ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish cases where complex mental states are analyzable into elements (composition) from those where elements coalesce (generation). Even when generated, these complex phenomena require direct study.

rubrics_metrics.name: Requirement of Method of Agreement and Difference for causal claims
rubrics_metrics.description: To prove that a complex mental phenomenon is generated by certain associated ideas, one must use the Method of Agreement and then confirm causation by the Method of Difference (e.g., show that associating the candidate cause with a previously indifferent action produces the new feeling).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Agreement alone (finding the putative causes present when effect occurs) is not sufficient; controlled contrasts (difference) are necessary to establish true causal laws of mind, especially for higher phenomena like belief or moral emotion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generated explanations do not replace direct experimental study
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if complex mental phenomena can be shown to be generated from simpler ones, this does not supersede the necessity of experimentally studying the generated phenomenon itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of constituent elements (e.g., sensations) does not allow deduction of all properties of the complex outcome (analogy to chemistry: knowing oxygen and sulphur does not yield sulphuric acid without specific study). Psychologists must still observe sequences and laws of the complex phenomena directly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sources of individual differences in mental susceptibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Different minds are susceptible in very different degrees to the same psychological causes; these differences may be (1) original/ultimate, (2) consequences of previous mental history (habit/education), or (3) depend on varieties of physical organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Investigations must analyze these sources rather than accept coarse empirical generalizations. Apparent mental differences can often be explained by differences in the intensity/quality of underlying sensations or prior associative histories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character, habit, and confirmed purpose as criteria for moral freedom
rubrics_metrics.description: A habit of willing (a purpose) which has become independent of feelings of pain or pleasure constitutes a confirmed character; the feeling that one could alter one’s character if one wished is the feeling of moral freedom.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Moral freedom is experienced when one feels habits and temptations are not one’s masters and when one’s wishes are strong enough to conquer contrary character in particular cases. Complete freedom requires success in shaping character by previous efforts.
